seo.title: Zynthian: plugin-hostd as its plugin host | OpenMixer
seo.description: Zynthian running its LV2 and CLAP plugins under plugin-hostd: what it is, what it changes, how to install and use it, the measured figures and where it stands.

hero.title: Zynthian: plugin-hostd as its plugin host.
hero.lede: How to install it, how to use it, what it changes in Zynthian and where it stands. The method and every table are in the technical notes linked at the end.

what.title: What it is.
what.p1: Zynthian is an open synthesizer and effects platform on a Raspberry Pi. It runs LV2 plugins through its own engines: mod-host, behind MOD-UI, which runs its effect chains, and jalv, which runs one plugin per process. plugin-hostd speaks mod-host's protocol and runs each plugin, LV2 or CLAP, in a worker process, so a plugin that crashes takes down only its own worker, which is put back with its settings. A whole chain can run in one worker instead of one process per plugin, and plugin-qualify measures each plugin on the device first, so the menus are built from what it found.
what.p2: With it Zynthian gets a plugin-hostd engine beside jalv for LV2 and CLAP plugins in chains, plugin-hostd as a switchable replacement for mod-host under MOD-UI, plugin menus ordered and tagged from per-plugin qualification records, and chains whose plugins the daemon groups into as few workers as their pins allow.

changes.title: How much it changes in Zynthian.
changes.p1: Nothing in Zynthian depends on it. It stays on jackd: no file that configures JACK changes, and no PipeWire is involved. As offered to Zynthian, the plugin-hostd engine stays off until a user turns it on, and MOD-UI keeps mod-host until a user switches its backend; going back is the same setting.
changes.p2: FreeMixer's forks of zynthian-ui and zynthian-sys have it on: plugin-hostd is the default plugin engine, in place of jalv, and MOD-UI's default backend, in place of mod-host, and the qualification sync is enabled. Every LV2 and CLAP plugin is listed once, under plugin-hostd and marked (PH). A plugin our host refuses stays in the list, marked not working, with its reason; nothing moves it to jalv. jalv remains an engine you can select.
changes.p3: What runs when nobody uses it: the interface starts a daemon only when a chain holds a plugin-hostd plugin. What stays enabled is the qualification sync, two minutes after boot at the lowest CPU and disk priority, skipping every plugin whose files have not changed, and omx-panel's MOD GUI and complement syncs. All of them can be disabled; the first sync on a device with many plugins is long.

image.title: The image
image.where: ZynthianOS Vangelis for the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5, with the forks of zynthian-ui and zynthian-sys, the OpenMixer apt repository, and plugin-hostd, omx-clap-host, omx-plugins, omx-panel and plugin-qualify installed and made the default. It is built from upstream's released Vangelis image with the fork's own update steps, as the fork's docs/openmixer-image.md describes, and will be a release of FreeMixer's zynthian-sys fork, in parts with their sums. It is not published yet: until it is, install the packages on a Vangelis you already run, as below.
image.firstBoot: The first boot does what any Zynthian card does once: it detects the kit, regenerates the SSH keys and the web certificate, creates the Wi-Fi access point, grows the file system to the card, and reboots once. Two minutes after boot the qualification sync starts in the background, at the lowest priority, and does not hold the boot; with the qualification records package installed it only checks that the plugin files are the ones the records describe.

existing.title: On an existing Vangelis
existing.p1: A Vangelis system already running needs no new image. As root, add the OpenMixer repository and install the packages:
existing.p2: openmixer-release carries the signing key and the apt source of the running Debian release. This enables no service: mod-host, MOD-UI, jalv and the menus stay as they were until you switch them.

switch.title: Turn it on, and back off
switch.p1: Three settings, each undone by setting it back:

use.title: Use it.
use.intro: With the plugin-hostd engine on, a plugin's menu entry ends in "(PH)". Select a chain, open its options and use Add Audio-FX processor; the plugin's controller pages follow its own sections.

group.title: A group: plugins in series in one worker
group.p1: With grouping on, a run of plugins in series in a chain shares one worker process and one JACK client instead of one process each. A group is what the chain has in series with nothing between: a parallel slot, the mixer strip or a jalv plugin ends it. A processor that runs alone has a Grouping entry in its options saying why.
group.p2: Grouping is off unless you set it. It saves most of the memory of one process per plugin: 24 plugins in one chain take about 64 MB, against about 110 MB under mod-host.

strip.title: A channel strip as plugins
strip.p1: EQ and dynamics per chain are ordinary effects in that chain; Zynthian's mixer keeps its level, pan and sends. Either add separate plugins (omx keyed-gate, omx eq8, omx comp: you choose each one and its order, and eq8 has eight bands), or one plugin, omx strip: input trim, filters, a gate, four EQ bands and a compressor in stereo, in one load and one worker, its five stages in any order.

mixbus.title: Shared effects on a Mixbus
mixbus.p1: One effect on a bus instead of one per chain, fed from each chain with Zynthian's own sends:
mixbus.step1: Add a chain and choose Mixbus. In its options, Add Audio-FX processor: omx reverb, then omx delay, each "(PH)".
mixbus.step2: In each chain that should feed it, open the mixer processor's controller page and raise the send level for that Mixbus, pre or post fader.
mixbus.p2: A plugin-hostd plugin behaves in a Mixbus as in any chain. A slot holds one processor or several, and several are parallel; a worker runs its plugins in series in one JACK client, so with grouping on:

series.runs: A and B in one worker, one JACK client

parallel.runs: a worker each: B and C are parallel, three clients

mixed.runs: A with B, a worker each for C and D, E with F: four clients

strip.runs: a worker each: the strip is in the signal's way

jalv.runs: a worker each, and the jalv plugin's own client

mixbus.p3: Send levels, pre and post fader, and pinning or moving a Mixbus are Zynthian's mixer and chain manager: none of them sends anything to the daemon. Measured at JACK ports, series, parallel and Mixbus chains give the levels they should: unity in series, +6.02 dB for two in parallel, the strip's -20 dB where it sits.

why.title: Why
why.p1: A Pi 5 has four cores. A synth plays many voices at once, and every block of audio has a deadline: all the voices must be computed before it is due. Run one after another, they all use one core. That core sets how many notes you can play, however idle the other three are.
why.p2: Some synths split their voices into tasks and ask the host to run them (CLAP's thread-pool extension). Tasks like that can run side by side, if the host lets them.

how.title: How it works
how.p1: omx-clap-host starts helper threads: one for each core the plugin's worker may use, minus one, because the audio thread takes the last core. Each helper is pinned to its core, runs at the audio thread's real-time priority and sleeps between blocks.
how.p2: When the plugin asks for its tasks, the helpers and the audio thread take them one by one, and the call returns when the last is done. If the priority cannot be set, there are no helpers and the tasks run as before, in turn.

gate.title: Who gets helpers
gate.p1: Not every plugin. Helper threads are given plugin by plugin, never everywhere. A plugin gets them only if its qualification found it real-time safe, with the helpers watched too, and faster with them. A task that allocates or waits on a lock would make every core miss the deadline.
gate.p2: Any other plugin runs as before: its tasks one after another on the audio thread. A plugin that gets helpers runs in a worker of its own, which plugin-hostd starts with the pool on.

switch.title: How to switch it
switch.p1: It is an option of omx-clap-host:
switch.qualified: qualified (the default): only plugins whose qualification grants it get helpers. plugin-hostd gives each worker the right setting, so on Zynthian you do not set it.
switch.on: on: every plugin that uses the extension gets helpers.
switch.off: off: every plugin runs its tasks in turn.

measured.title: What it gives
measured.p1: Measured on a Raspberry Pi 5 at 48 kHz and 256 frames, so the block is due in 5333 µs. The plugin is a test plugin that splits each block into 16 tasks, because no plugin on the Pi asks for tasks yet, Surge XT included. The time is the mean cost of one block, with the helpers off and on:
measured.p2: At 512 frames, the 48-voice load takes 6.6 ms of the 10.7 ms block with the helpers off and 1.7 ms with them on. No block went over its deadline in any run.
measured.p3: This is the best case: equal tasks that share nothing. A real instrument has not been measured with it, so there is no Surge XT figure. Surge XT does not split its voices, and for it the cores come from running each instrument in a worker of its own: four instances with 16 notes each ran at 14 to 15 % of a core each.

status.intro: Everything below is still to be measured on the device. What is released, merged or coming is in the cards after it.

series.title: Where the changes to Zynthian stand.
series.forks: The engine and the system changes are carried on FreeMixer's forks of zynthian-ui and zynthian-sys. In zynthian-ui: the plugin-hostd engine and its client for plugin-hostd's protocol 0.4, plugin-hostd by default with a snapshot converter, menus from qualification, chains from the daemon's planner. In zynthian-sys: the OpenMixer repository, plugin-hostd as the mod-host of MOD-UI, MOD GUIs from omx-panel, OpenMixer in the default install. Merged and open pull requests are listed on each fork.
series.upstream: Upstream, one change is proposed so far: building MOD-UI's environment on Python 3.13, in zynthian-sys. The rest has not been proposed to Zynthian's maintainers yet.
